reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant predisposition to gastrointestinal stromal tumours caused by germline activating variants in KIT or, less often, PDGFRA
Affected families develop multiple GISTs, typically at a younger age than sporadic cases, most commonly in the stomach and small intestine
Tumours arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal and characteristically express KIT (CD117) on immunohistochemistry
Associated features in some kindreds include diffuse hyperplasia of interstitial cells of Cajal, cutaneous hyperpigmentation, mastocytosis and dysphagia
Presentation may include gastrointestinal bleeding, abdominal mass, obstruction or an incidental submucosal lesion
Because the tumours are driven by constitutive receptor tyrosine-kinase signalling, tyrosine-kinase inhibition is the principal systemic therapy for GIST
Genetic counselling and surveillance are important given the dominant inheritance and multiplicity of tumours
reference.pathophysiology: Familial gastrointestinal stromal tumour syndrome is driven by germline activating variants in the receptor tyrosine-kinase genes KIT or PDGFRA. These variants cause ligand-independent, constitutive activation of the receptor and its downstream proliferative signalling pathways in the interstitial cells of Cajal, the gut pacemaker cells from which GISTs derive. The inherited mutation predisposes to hyperplasia of these cells and to the development of multiple stromal tumours throughout the gastrointestinal tract, often at an earlier age than sporadic disease. The specific germline variant influences tumour distribution, associated phenotypic features and sensitivity to targeted tyrosine-kinase inhibition.
additionalDifferentials: Carney triad and Carney-Stratakis syndrome (SDH-deficient GIST)
Leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma of the gut
Neuroendocrine tumours of the gastrointestinal tract
additionalInvestigations: Endoscopy and endoscopic ultrasound to characterise submucosal lesions
Cross-sectional imaging for tumour staging and surveillance
Histology with KIT (CD117) and DOG1 immunohistochemistry
Germline and tumour molecular testing for KIT and PDGFRA variants
Family history assessment, genetic counselling and cascade testing of relatives
redFlags: Gastrointestinal haemorrhage or anaemia from an ulcerated tumour
Bowel obstruction or a rapidly enlarging abdominal mass
Features suggesting metastatic spread such as hepatic lesions
Multiple or early-onset tumours indicating a hereditary syndrome requiring family evaluation
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on tumour size, mitotic activity, site and resectability; localised tumours may be cured surgically while advanced disease is managed with tyrosine-kinase inhibition. The hereditary predisposition means new tumours can arise over time, so long-term surveillance is required.
pitfalls: Assuming a GIST is sporadic and missing a hereditary syndrome in a patient with multiple or early tumours
Failing to arrange genetic counselling and family screening once a germline variant is identified
Overlooking SDH-deficient and NF1-associated GISTs, which behave and respond differently
Not confirming KIT/DOG1 status, risking misclassification of the mesenchymal tumour
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
